## 1. Energy audit

![](images/Clipboard.png){width=15%}

**The "greenest" kilowatt-hour is the one you never use.**

Before investing in solar panels, doing an [energy
audit](https://creationcare.github.io/Sustainable_Church/energy-audit.html)
can significantly reduce your electricity usage, and lead to designing a
smaller, more affordable system.

## 2. Who do you call?

![](images/SUN-Logo-Gradient.png){width=35%}

To find reputable solar companies in your area, contact [Solar United
Neighbors](https://solarunitedneighbors.org/ready-set-solar/nonprofits/).
They are a non-profit committed to helping people find the right
companies to do their solar panel analysis and installation.

## 3. Groundwork

![](images/Groundwork.png){width=25%}

To begin the analysis, you will need the following:

1.  12 months worth of electric bills. This will be the basis for
    analyzing potential savings, and will also allow you to assess the
    accuracy of the model used to determine savings.

2.  Does your local utility offer or allow "net metering" of some sort?
    This can have a large impact on the size of the system you should build.

    For example, TXU, Green Mountain, Octopus, Reliant, and Gexa are
    some of the larger providers that have some sort of power buyback
    program - though all are different. Austin Energy provides true 1:1
    net metering. If you are served by a co-op, then your choices may be
    very limited.

3.  Consider what a suitable location for solar panels might be. The
    ideal location is a sloped roof of about 20 degrees, facing south;
    but a flat roof, or a roof whose slope faces some other direction
    can also be used. A ground mounted system is also feasible, if there
    is sufficient land to place it on. For perhaps 50% more up-front
    expense, a parking lot could be covered. The location should see
    little to no shade during the day, especially around mid-day.

4.  If you have "smart meters", then you should be able to download
    usage data for every 15 minutes, which can tell you a lot more about
    how your usage peaks and the potential for savings. Learn more at
    the [Smart Meter](https://www.smartmetertexas.com/home) website.
    
##  4. Working with a contractor

![](images/Contractor.png){width=25%}

If net metering is not available for you, then make certain that the design your 
contractor develops does not produce more power than the maximum usage you have
seen during the year. This is where the 15 minute usage data can become 
extremely useful.

Ask how the usage information was factored into the analysis. For many, the 
highest usage should be on Sundays, with lower usage during the week, unless
you have a school or other weekday usage. With net metering, there is a real
opportunity to sell power during the week.

In calculating the economics, a key input is how much electric rates are
expected to rise over the life of the system - which should be about 25 years.
Based on the projections from 
[TEPRI](https://tepri.org/2025/12/affordabilitypaper/), a reasonable projection
is for rates to increase by one &#162; per kWh for about 10 years, and then stay
flat. 

## 5. Financials
![](images/Sun_dollars.png){width=25%}

### Economics of the installation

When the plan is done, it should have an undiscounted payback period of less 
than 12-15 years, and hopefully quite a bit lower than that. You should also
qualify for the 30% "direct pay" incentive payments from the IRS for a 
non-profit. Similarly, the ROI (Return On Investment) should be greater than
about 5%, and perhaps even into double digits.

### Financing

The Diocese generally tries to discourage congregations from acquiring loans
that put a lien on the church property, so that avenue is probably not feasible.
However, there are opportunities for financing where the lien is placed on the 
solar panels themselves, and that is entirely acceptable. (I need a reference here)
